article_text:
Ryan Frigillana: Tears, Blood, Sweat

©Ryan Frigillana, The House They Built, 2022

How do memory, images, and systems of belief shape lived experience and a sense of belonging?

This question is at the heart of Tears, Blood, Sweat, in which Ryan Frigillana reconsiders the American Dream through intertwined histories of land, labor, and citizenship. Drawing on his experience as a first-generation Filipino American, he interweaves personal and family histories with broader sociopolitical narratives.

Co-curated by Helen Trompeteler and Leo Hsu, the exhibition at Silver Eye Center of Photography , brings together three interconnected bodies of work that explore displacement, belonging, and memory through distinct photographic strategies. Helen Trompeteler recently spoke with Ryan about the experiences, ideas, and questions that connect these projects. Tears, Blood, Sweat continues through November 7, 2026.

An interview with Helen Trompeteler and Ryan Frigillana follows.

HT: It’s so good to see you again, Ryan. I wanted to start with Balikbayan, which opens the exhibition. This body of work explores your desire to return to the Philippines, using studio still lifes, collage, and tableau to explore your connection to family and homeland. In The House They Built for example, an archival photograph of your grandparents forms the foundation of a deck of cards, introducing tensions between family love, stability, and precarity.

What role does the family album play in Balikbayan, and how do collage or staging allow you to reimagine it?

RF : Thanks for having me and for this lovely conversation. The family album was my introduction to photography. Most people engage with the family album in a book-like form, and that’s how I came to know of photography’s utility from the way my family used it.

Balikbayan differs from other projects which usually begin with a question or curiosity. I was so used to working in a traditional documentary mode for most of my practice, making images intuitively out in the field with my family. Before then, I rarely staged images and felt that staging or intervening was a big no-no for me. With Balikbayan, I really wanted to try something different by leading with a process-based endeavor. The questions came afterward. It was the inverse of my normal way of making.

It started with this curiosity about what I could do with props and staging. I’d experimented with still lifes before, but I wanted to use things that were available to me in relation to my family and history, things that tied me back to my home in the Philippines. This meant working with the tangible family pictures and albums that I had access to, and playing with the physicality of the images.

The House They Built was a spontaneous image. My niece had come over, and we were playing with cards on the table. After my brother had dropped her off at her mother’s, I noticed the pile of cards lying on the table with the picnic tablecloth, and I started building a little house structure. We had also been looking at pictures from the Philippines, including photographs of my grandparents, and then I just started playing with those too.

For me, the project is about play and experimenting. I’m not imposing a rigid set of rules for myself in terms of what this project should or could be. I think that by having fun, and then allowing yourself to just explore things freely, maybe from there things can escalate into more serious questions.

HT: Thank you for sharing that, I love that you were driven by process and intuition, and that work evolved out of your relationship with your niece. That’s really beautiful.

Ryan Frigillana, Family Tree (after Rockwell), 2022

HT: I’d like to explore this process-driven approach further through Family Tree (after Rockwell), which layers Norman Rockwell’s The Graduate, originally published as an illustration for The Saturday Evening Post, with family photographs. Your hand and loupe also appear on a lightbox, making the process of looking and assembling visible.

Could you talk about how the lightbox and its interplay of opacity and luminance shape the piece, and what you hope this dimension offers the viewer?

RF: I think the lightbox serves two purposes. It allows for the opacity to shine through, showing the physical layering of objects on the surface. But I also wanted to allude to the idea of scrutiny, as if you were examining something scientifically on a table.

I was thinking about this two-pronged notion of hypervisibility and invisibility, as someone who comes into this country. Invisibility meaning you often feel alienated, maybe unheard or unseen. But there’s also this aspect of hypervisibility, where you’re very conscious of how you carry yourself or present yourself to others. For me, that’s what the lightbox and loupe allude to.

The Rockwell images, though, I don’t think I’ve ever mentioned this to you, but it really came from when I first moved into my family home on Long Island. The previous homeowners were an elderly couple from a very different time and background from my family. When they moved, they left behind this trove of books and materials in the basement and the garage, including Norman Rockwell books and illustrated encyclopedias for boys and girls. These were the visual materials from the 60s and 70s that I trained my eye on as a young child, and they informed the way I viewed myself in relation to being American. That visual experience was very formative for me.

Using the Norman Rockwell images was a way for me to impose my own family’s presence into this storied culture of what America could or should be, and how it views itself. The opacity also speaks to the unseen moments of care and tenderness that we share amongst ourselves, yet aren’t visible to the public eye.

©Ryan Frigillana, Memories of a Body, 2023

HT: Invisibility is something I’ve thought about a lot in relation to this exhibition. In Kung Ano Ang Nagpapakain Sa Iyo (What Feeds You) , for example, one of our first encounters with your mother is through her gestures of care shown in shadow. Later, in Memories of a Body , we see the indentations her body leaves behind on the couch, her presence isn’t seen but deeply felt. In PATMOS , you never make the president fully visible.

I’m interested in how invisibility operates differently across the exhibition, as both a form of care and a form of resistance. Could you talk more about that tension between presence and absence?

RF: Yeah, I guess I’m not really consciously thinking about these dynamics. What I’m trying to say is that, when I’m creating work, I sometimes make things invisible to protect my family.

In the case of the PATMOS images, it was also a way of protecting myself from the barrage of media I was experiencing. Sometimes, for me, omitting presence is a way of either amplifying someone’s presence through imagination, or protecting them. With the PATMOS images, Trump is this larger-than-life figure. We all know what he looks like, but I was more focused on how this person’s presence makes you feel and on the guttural reaction to the images.

©Ryan Frigillana, Keeper, 2021

HT : Labor is an important thread throughout the exhibition, particularly the legacy of Filipino labor at key moments in American history. At a pivotal moment in the exhibition you recontextualized an image by Dorothea Lange of migrant workers in California. In Manong , you explore these histories through your own family experience.

Could you talk about how you approach these histories of labor in relation to your family?

RF: The Manong project really started with photographing my father in his garden. Sometimes for me, a body of work doesn’t always start with a question, but with doing something, an accumulation of a behavior. So, I was repeatedly photographing my father while he was tending to his garden, and initially I didn’t know why I was drawn to that. Partly, it was a way to spend time with him, so the camera became a bridge for our relationship.

But from there, I started to ask broader questions. Why was I drawn to agrarian labor and this act of caring and tending to one’s land? And what does that mean for Filipinos now, or for Filipinos in the past? From there, I started digging deeper into the legacies of tending to land as a Filipino here in America. That’s what brought me to the FSA images in the Library of Congress archives, where I found the Dorothea Lange image.

When I came across the FSA images online, I was struck by how that experience and history had been flattened. I wanted to learn more about the people depicted in these fields, who were hunched over and laboring, and who I felt had essentially been flattened into silhouettes, one homogenous idea of migrant labor. I think those people were more than just labor, and I wanted to humanize them: to understand who they were, their stories, their histories, and the families they left behind.

So, in asking those questions, I did my own research, trying to fill in the gaps I felt were missing, but I couldn’t fill them. So I did it with my own family by looking at my mother’s story, which I felt paralleled that of the Manong generation who came in the early 1930s to work in the fields. My mother came in the late 1980s as a nurse. I was thinking about the parallels in the extraction of labor, and that’s something I’m still exploring with this project. It’s ongoing. As I make and collect more images, more questions arise, and I just follow where those questions take me.

HT: I think your work offers a counterpoint to those historical photographic surveys, which, as you say, often turned individuals into symbols for broader narratives, obscuring their individual experiences. Your work reintroduces a sense of care and individuality in a really moving way.

Installation view of Tears, Blood, Sweat, featuring PATMOS. Photograph by Sean Carroll

HT : I’d like to turn to PATMOS , which breaks news imagery down into its constituent elements of pixels and halftone dots, challenging their authority.

How did you approach translating these disrupted images into the exhibition space, and what kind of physical encounter did you want to create for viewers?

RF: I think the embodied experience was something I was thinking a lot about when putting together that installation. When I first made those images from screen captures during the 2020 and 2024 presidential elections, I felt like I was being swallowed by those images and totally engulfed. I wanted to recreate that sort of frenzy and the feeling of overwhelm I experienced, as well as the trepidation I felt for the future. It’s almost like an assault on the senses.

With the book, I tried as hard as I could to recreate that feeling through full-bleed pages in a large format. But being able to translate that into physical space only amplified it for me. The physical embodiment of the work as an installation really communicated the feelings I was trying to create effectively.

Scale was important with the vinyl pieces. I really wanted people to think not just about their physical proximity to images, but also about the proximity of images in their lives. When you get closer to the print, the image loses its potency in a way. It becomes difficult to read. Maybe I want people to think about their relationship to images in that regard: the closer you get, the more you understand how images work, and the more you’re able to think about the motives behind them.

HT: Very much so. It feels as though, by revealing how images are constructed, you’re inviting viewers to reflect on their role in society and their personal relationship to the images around them.

Since you began the project, how have your thoughts on the authority of images and questions of agency and control around them shifted? Has your sense of art’s capacity to address or bridge divides, whether personal or ideological, changed, too?

RF: I think it’s become more dire now than ever. Media literacy is more important than ever, especially with so much disinformation and the rise of artificial images. I mean, that’s a whole other topic.

When I was making PATMOS , I was thinking about the way images shape behavior and how they sell you a certain notion of idealism. Bringing in biblical imagery was a way of speaking to the dangers of that. I grew up in a very religious background, and I think a lot about how, as a kid, I was trained on these images of utopia and heaven, an ideal universe and way of life. But alongside these utopian images in the Bible were images of violence, trauma, and fear.

I’m thinking about the contemporary images that swim around us now, and about American idealism as something sold to us as an ideal, a utopia. There’s this idea of America as a democratic ideal, with justice and equality as its selling points. But I don’t often see that reflected in reality, so I’m trying to show you what I experience and feel as a person here in America.

HT: I really appreciate your openness in sharing how PATMOS is a very visceral expression of what it feels like to live in the world we’re living in.

Do you feel that Manong and Balikbayan offer another kind of utopia? A utopia rooted in family, love, and connection to the generations before us?

RF : Yes, I mean, I would hope so. I hope there’s something to redeem from that experience, because if not, then I don’t know what the point of making the work would be for me.

By bookending the exhibition with Manong and Balikbayan , I hope people come away with the sense that family and community are larger than whatever the experiences of PATMOS are inflicting on us, psychologically and physically. Family and community are always the bookends to things. You can always come and go and return. They will be there, as you said, as our utopia, our safe haven, and the spaces where we actually are safe.

I think the point of PATMOS for me is that politicians won’t save you. I think the real salvation lies in the people in your communities, the communities you build and foster, and your families. So, I hope people get a sense of that hope, and of those pockets of light they can see in their own lives.

©Ryan Frigillana, Mother’s Faith, 2022

HT : Absolutely, thank you for sharing that, Ryan. For me, it’s been so palpable that those two projects provide a foundation for navigating this in-between world, which can often feel disorientating. Thank you. I have just one final question.

This exhibition brings Balikbayan , PATMOS , and Manong into conversation for the first time. Each body of work has emerged through its own process of discovery, yet they feel very interconnected and continually unfolding.

Has bringing these works together for the first time changed your understanding of them, either individually or collectively? And has seeing them in conversation opened up new directions for your practice?

RF : I don’t know if it’s changed the way I see them individually, but I think it’s caused me to reflect on my practice as a whole. The exhibition has given me an opportunity to step back and see what I’m curious about each time, and the language I’m building with each successive body of work.

Maybe that’s something I wasn’t fully conscious of before. When I’m making a body of work, I’m just following an intuition or a curiosity, and I’m not necessarily thinking about what I made before. Now, I’m thinking more about building on a language and a way of questioning.

I don’t know where that will take me. I’m still working on several projects, but I think it’s given me a sense of direction in terms of why I’m curious about certain things. It’s given me some clarity, and maybe I can use this experience of the exhibition to help further build the language that I’m creating for myself for future projects.

HT: Thank you so much, Ryan. I really appreciate the chance to be in conversation with you again.

RF : Thank you. It’s lovely to catch up and speak, and to think about this work. You know, every time I get to talk about it, something shifts or clarifies in me. So I always relish these opportunities. So, thank you.

HT : Thank you!

Ryan Frigillana (b. Iligan City, Philippines) is a lens-based artist working between Long Island,New York, and Southaven, Mississippi. Drawing from an upbringing shaped by migration and Adventism, he combines photographs with reworked materials—including print media, family and public archives, and biblical illustrations from his childhood—to address the tensions and continuities of diaspora and faith.

Through books and installations, he approaches photography as a form of evidence, allegory, and prayer: as record, symbol, and confession.Frigillana has exhibited at Light Work, Houston Center for Photography, Blue Sky Oregon Centerfor the Photographic Arts, and Candela Photographic Arts. He is a recipient of the NYSCA/NYFA Artist Fellowship in Photography (‘25), the JGS Fellowship for Photography (‘25, ‘21), theAperture & Google Creator Labs Photo Fund (‘23), and the En Foco Photography Fellowship(‘23), and has completed residencies through the Penumbra Workspace Program (‘24) and the Penumbra Foundation Risograph Print & Publication Residency (‘21). His work has been published by Aperture, Atlanta Center for Photography, Humble Arts Foundation, Booooooom, PhMuseum, Der Greif, Musée magazine, and The New Yorker among others. He holds a BFA inPhotography and Related Media (2020) from the Fashion Institute of Technology.

Silver Eye Center for Photography is the Pittsburgh region’s only nonprofit institution dedicated exclusively to contemporary photography. Our mission is to promote the power of contemporary photography as a fine art medium by creating original exhibitions, unique educational programming, and a space for artists to learn, create, and connect through our digital lab and education center, The Lab @ Silver Eye. Our programs are dedicated to supporting the work of emerging, mid-career, and under-recognized artists and sharing that work with our diverse audience in engaging and meaningful ways.

title_original: The Bicentenary of Photography – Drawing Lab: Eclipse
editorial_excerpt_zh: 值摄影两百周年之际，群展 Eclipse 在 Drawing Lab 探讨摄影与绘画之间的关系——[…] 本文《摄影两百周年——Drawing Lab：Eclipse》最初发表于 The Eye of Photography……
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "值摄影两百周年之际，群展 Eclipse 在 Drawing Lab 探讨摄影与绘画之间的关系。Drawing Lab 是一个致力于当代绘画实验与推广的场所，位于巴黎 75001，rue de Richelieu 17 号。通过图形聚焦、感知模糊与感光装置，绘画在其各个维度上浮现于摄影的阴影之中，揭示其物质性、用途，以及图像得以生成的种种过程。展览汇集了标志性作品、近期作品与新的互动装置。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "参展艺术家包括 Fabienne Ballandras、Léa Belooussovitch、Mireille Blanc、Nicolas Daubanes、Jean Olivier Hucleux、Éric Manigaud、Célia Muller、Daphné Nan Le Sergent、Pascal Navarro 和 Jérémie Setton。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "由 Anne Favier 策展。展览于 2026 年 9 月 25 日至 2027 年 1 月 3 日展出。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当 Nicéphore Niépce 于 1826 年发明摄影成像时，与他同时代的 Henry Fox Talbot 也相信，他通过摄影发现了一支“忠实的铅笔”，能够自然地捕捉光与影的书写。他同样将光敏印相——通过直接接触获得的光敏印痕——称为“photogenic drawings”，这是摄影作为固定并暂时遮蔽光线之过程的早期表现。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "如今，摄影被公认为主要艺术媒介之一。本次群展试图凸显摄影与各种形式的当代绘画之间所保持的紧密对话，并展示绘画如何在这项两百年之久的发明的阴影中继续发展并重新发明自身。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在摄影与后摄影生成绝大多数图像的时代，一些从事绘画的艺术家与摄影源图像保持着惊人的接近，有时以非凡的忠实度复制或转译它们。如此一来，他们创作出具有非凡上镜品质的绘画，促使观者质疑自己看到的究竟是图形图像还是摄影图像。但为什么要花这么多时间重绘一张快照？将摄影图像转译为绘画，首先是一个揭示的过程：文献变成有待审视、挖掘和转化的表面——用 Jean Olivier Hucleux 的话说，是“transmuted”（嬗变）。尽管绘图者在复制图像的过程中倾向于抹去自身，他们同时揭示并强化摄影的痕迹——细节、颗粒、质感、表面、物质性与脆弱性——并赋予图像一种新的持续感与触感。通过 Jean Olivier Hucleux 的一件历史作品，以及 Daphné Nan Le Sergent、Mireille Blanc、Éric Manigaud 和 Célia Muller 更近期的作品，展览试图让这种“图像的石墨化生成”变得可感，借用 Jean-Christophe Bailly 用于描述向绘画过渡的表达。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "摄影图像也可能通过各种图形转译过程而遮蔽自身：模糊（Léa Belooussovitch）、“盲”转录、叠加、关联或并置（Fabienne Ballandras）。这些视觉偏移产生新的焦点调整与观看距离、感知中断——有时导致不可辨识或抽象——并开启对摄影图像的批判性视角，尤其是媒体传播的那些图像，从标志性新闻照片到伴随它们的图注。绘画由此赋予这些图像新的物质性、可见性与时间性。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "通过呈现复杂的摄影—图形装置、Nicolas Daubanes 的白炽印相、Jérémie Setton 的一件互动装置——其中观者在揭示图像时扮演双重角色——以及 Pascal Navarro 随时间逐渐显现的感光作品，展览也通过绘画探索摄影的奠基性原则：潜像、显影、定影、可复制性、负像与正像的可逆性、感光化与印痕。通过这些实验性作品，绘画本身变得具有摄影性。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "一件历史作品、标志性与实验性作品、新委约创作，以及为 Drawing Lab 重新激活的装置汇聚在一起，在三个主题部分——“石墨化生成”、“焦点调整”和“潜像”——之间形成对话。通过这些共鸣，Eclipse 揭示绘画在与摄影相遇时如何受到考验、转化并重新定义。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Drawing Lab 17, rue de Richelieu — 75001 Paris drawinglabparis.com @drawinglabparis", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "每日 11.00 至 19.00", "translated": true}]
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "On the occasion of the Bicentennial of Photography, the group exhibition Eclipse explores the relationship between photography and drawing at the Drawing Lab — a venue dedicated to the experimentation and promotion of contemporary drawing, located at 17 rue de Richelieu, 75001 Paris. Through graphic focalisations, perceptual blurring and photosensitive devices, drawing, in all its dimensions, emerges in the shadow of photography, revealing its materiality, its uses, and the very processes through which images come into being. The exhibition brings together emblematic works, recent pieces and new interactive installations."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Featuring works of Fabienne Ballandras, Léa Belooussovitch, Mireille Blanc, Nicolas Daubanes, Jean Olivier Hucleux, Éric Manigaud, Célia Muller, Daphné Nan Le Sergent, Pascal Navarro and Jérémie Setton."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Curated by Anne Favier. Exhibition on view from 25 September 2026 to 3 January 2027."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "While Nicéphore Niépce invented photographic image-making in 1826, his contemporary Henry Fox Talbot also believed he had discovered, through photography, a “faithful pencil” capable of naturally capturing the writing of shadows and light. He likewise referred to photograms, light- sensitive impressions obtained through direct contact, as “photogenic drawings”, early manifestationsof photography as a process of fixing and momentarily obscuring light."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Today, photography is recognised as one of the major artistic mediums. This group exhibition seeks to highlight the close dialogue it maintains with contemporary drawing in all its forms, and to show how drawing continues to develop and reinvent itself in the shadow of this two-hundred-year- old invention."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "At a time when photography and post-photography generate the vast majority of images, some artists working with drawing maintain a striking proximity to photographic source-images, sometimes reproducing or translating them with remarkable fidelity. In doing so, they create drawings of extraordinary photogenic quality, prompting viewers to question whether they are looking at a graphic or photographic image. But why spend so much time redrawing a snapshot? The transfer of a photographic image into drawing is above all a process of revelation: the document becomes a surface to be scrutinised, excavated and transformed—“transmuted”, in the words of Jean Olivier Hucleux. While the draughtsperson tends to efface themselves in the act of reproducing the image, they simultaneously reveal and intensify the traces of the photographic—detail, grain, texture, surface, materiality and fragility—while endowing the image with a new sense of duration and tactility. Through a historical work by Jean Olivier Hucleux and more recent works by Daphné Nan Le Sergent, Mireille Blanc, Éric Manigaud and Célia Muller, the exhibition seeks to make tangible this “graphite becoming of the image”, to borrow Jean-Christophe Bailly’s expression for the passage into drawing."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The photographic image may also eclipse itself through various processes of graphic transposition: blurring (Léa Belooussovitch), “blind” transcription, superimposition, association or juxtaposition (Fabienne Ballandras). These visual shifts generate new focal adjustments and viewing distances, perceptual disruptions—sometimes leading to illegibility or abstraction—and open up critical perspectives on photographic images, particularly those circulated by the media, from iconic press photographs to the captions that accompany them. article_text:
On the occasion of the Bicentennial of Photography, the group exhibition Eclipse explores the relationship between photography and drawing at the Drawing Lab — a venue dedicated to the experimentation and promotion of contemporary drawing, located at 17 rue de Richelieu, 75001 Paris. Through graphic focalisations, perceptual blurring and photosensitive devices, drawing, in all its dimensions, emerges in the shadow of photography, revealing its materiality, its uses, and the very processes through which images come into being. The exhibition brings together emblematic works, recent pieces and new interactive installations.

Featuring works of Fabienne Ballandras, Léa Belooussovitch, Mireille Blanc, Nicolas Daubanes, Jean Olivier Hucleux, Éric Manigaud, Célia Muller, Daphné Nan Le Sergent, Pascal Navarro and Jérémie Setton.

Curated by Anne Favier. Exhibition on view from 25 September 2026 to 3 January 2027.

While Nicéphore Niépce invented photographic image-making in 1826, his contemporary Henry Fox Talbot also believed he had discovered, through photography, a “faithful pencil” capable of naturally capturing the writing of shadows and light. He likewise referred to photograms, light- sensitive impressions obtained through direct contact, as “photogenic drawings”, early manifestationsof photography as a process of fixing and momentarily obscuring light.

Today, photography is recognised as one of the major artistic mediums. This group exhibition seeks to highlight the close dialogue it maintains with contemporary drawing in all its forms, and to show how drawing continues to develop and reinvent itself in the shadow of this two-hundred-year- old invention.

At a time when photography and post-photography generate the vast majority of images, some artists working with drawing maintain a striking proximity to photographic source-images, sometimes reproducing or translating them with remarkable fidelity. In doing so, they create drawings of extraordinary photogenic quality, prompting viewers to question whether they are looking at a graphic or photographic image. But why spend so much time redrawing a snapshot? The transfer of a photographic image into drawing is above all a process of revelation: the document becomes a surface to be scrutinised, excavated and transformed—“transmuted”, in the words of Jean Olivier Hucleux. While the draughtsperson tends to efface themselves in the act of reproducing the image, they simultaneously reveal and intensify the traces of the photographic—detail, grain, texture, surface, materiality and fragility—while endowing the image with a new sense of duration and tactility. Through a historical work by Jean Olivier Hucleux and more recent works by Daphné Nan Le Sergent, Mireille Blanc, Éric Manigaud and Célia Muller, the exhibition seeks to make tangible this “graphite becoming of the image”, to borrow Jean-Christophe Bailly’s expression for the passage into drawing.

The photographic image may also eclipse itself through various processes of graphic transposition: blurring (Léa Belooussovitch), “blind” transcription, superimposition, association or juxtaposition (Fabienne Ballandras). These visual shifts generate new focal adjustments and viewing distances, perceptual disruptions—sometimes leading to illegibility or abstraction—and open up critical perspectives on photographic images, particularly those circulated by the media, from iconic press photographs to the captions that accompany them. Drawing thus grants these images new materialities, visibilities and temporalities.

By presenting complex photo-graphic devices, Nicolas Daubanes’s incandescent photograms, an interactive installation by Jérémie Setton in which the viewer plays a double role in revealing the image, and Pascal Navarro’s photosensitive works that gradually emerge over time—the exhibition also explores, through drawing, the founding principles of photography: the latent image,development, fixation, reproducibility, the reversibility of negative and positive, photosensitisation and imprint. Through these experimental works, drawing itself becomes photographic.

A historical work, emblematic and experimental pieces, newly commissioned productions and installations reactivated for the Drawing Lab come together to form a dialogue across three thematic sections — “Graphite Becoming”, “Focal Adjustments” and “Latent Image”. Through these resonances, Eclipse reveals drawing as it is tested, transformed and redefined through itsencounter with photography.

Drawing Lab 17, rue de Richelieu — 75001 Paris drawinglabparis.com @drawinglabparis

Daily from 11.00 to 19.00

article_text:
Art Dhaka, a new fair bringing together traditional, modern and contemporary art founded by Durjoy Rahman, Fahd Sattar, Nahar Khan, and T. Aumia Khundkar, will have its inaugural edition from 6–10 November at Aloki in Dhaka.

The artists Najmun Nahar Keya and Zihan Karim will lead the curatorial direction of the fair. A dedicated print pavilion will be curated by the artist Fareha Zeba. A series of exhibitions, events and panel talks discussing the arts and culture landscape in Bangladesh will also take place throughout the week alongside the main fair.

editorial_excerpt_zh: 从 2026 年 12 月 5 日至 6 日到 2027 年 10 月 30 日至 31 日，克拉夫迪·斯卢班（Klavdij Sluban）将在巴黎市中心第九区的一个宽敞阁楼里，为业余和经验丰富的摄影师主持工作坊。这篇关于 2026-2027 Klavdij Sluban 大师班的文章最初出现在……

article_text:
From December 5 & 6, 2026, to October 30 & 31, 2027, Klavdij Sluban will be hosting amateur and experienced photographers for workshops in a spacious loft in the heart of Paris, in the 9th arrondissement. Registration for MK is now open.

The spirit of Le Masterklass is: “Show me your photos and I’ll tell you who you are”. Klavdij Sluban is internationally renowned for his journeys ever further east, as well as for his unique work around the world on adolescts in prison, with whom he creates photography workshops.

Le Masterklass is specific in that Klavdij’s individual guidance helps each participant to find their own personal photographic writing. After twelve months, a coherent, sensitive and meaningful body of work is created, in the form of a portfolio and book of a high standard – first and foremost for the participant’s own enjoyment, and subsequently to enter competitions, apply for grants and awards, and to be shown to photography professionals with a view to publication, a book, an exhibition… The cornerstone of the MK is image editing; however, writing texts will also have a prominent position in the project’s development.

In 2026, following several MK sessions, Marco Berti Palazzi was awarded the Escourbiac Prize – Fondation des Treilles, with the publication of a book whilst Camille-Renée Devid exhibited at the Rencontres d’Arles as the winner of the 2025 Portfolio Review.

With one session per month, three take place in a group at the loft in Paris, two are one-to-one in person at the loft in Paris, and seven are held online.

article_text:
‘H ated” is not putting it too strongly. The strength of feeling against Just Stop Oil , as caught by this documentary, is really disturbing. It’s filmed from inside the climate group’s protests, and as activists block roads, furious drivers hurl abuse. “Have a wash you fucking idiots!” “Middle class wankers!” It gets physical, too – punching, kicking and dragging. One man appears to drive his van at protesters. Another walks along a line of them, pouring water over their heads, one by one.

Film-maker Rich Felgate could not be closer to the action; his girlfriend, Indigo Rumbelow, is an activist. “Don’t look at the camera. I’m a fly on the wall,” he tells her at their shared house, where books about the suffragettes and Gandhi are on the shelves. On the streets, activists glue themselves to roads and fasten their necks together with bike locks. In October 2022, campaigners notoriously lobbed tomato soup at Van Gogh’s Sunflowers . At one road shutdown an angry driver shouts: “You’re children.” But they’re not all young; a vicar in late middle age with Parkinson’s quickly takes his medicine before he’s cuffed.

The group’s strategy is to stay disruptive, stay in the news. We watch Just Stop Oil spokespeople appear on TV in increasingly hostile interviews. Their argument is that the planet is in crisis, there is no time to lose. Piers Morgan et al tell them their message is lost in the tactics. And it does look like that: by targeting infrastructure that hits ordinary people rather than going at the fossil fuel industry directly, Just Stop Oil throws away goodwill generated towards protesters acting on their consciences. Still, they claim a victory when Labour wins the election in 2024, pledging no new licences for gas and oilfields. (It seems that last week’s go-ahead for the Jackdaw North Sea gasfield does not break that pledge, since it already holds a licence.)

As Just Stop Oil actions escalate, Rumbelow and other activists are arrested and jailed, handed down the longest-ever prison sentences in England for nonviolent protest. When the credits roll, you have to wonder who the real vandals are..

article_text:
Indio Downey , son of Robert Downey Jr, has booked his first lead role in a movie with indie pic Love In Vein .

Written and directed by Will De Los Santos ( Spun ), adapted from the late Ryan Leone novel Wasting Talent , the film is being produced by Muse Productions in association with ArtHouse Gooning, with principal photography scheduled to take place in LA in March and April 2027. Chris Hanley, whose producing credits include American Psycho , Spring Breakers and The Virgin Suicides , will produce alongside Orson Oblowitz, Tricia van Klaveren and Ben D. Wallace.

Downey will play Damien, the central character in De Los Santos’ adaptation of Leone’s “uncompromising” novel, who “navigates addiction, love and self-destruction…set against LA’s underground landscape, the film follows Damien through a fragile collision of drugs, relationships, music and survival as the people around him struggle with their own versions of desire, dependency and escape.”

Watch on Deadline

Related Stories

Adam Brody's 'Nobody Wants This' Mother Shares Thoughts On Pro-Palestine Comments: "You Take The Victim & Make The Victim The Perpetrator"

Everything We Know About 'The Gilded Age' Season 4 So Far

The film is being financed by Jeffrey Gliwa through Blue Shark Pictures, with Gliwa serving as executive producer. Additional casting is currently underway. “Ryan left behind a brutally honest novel about addiction, love and Los Angeles. Since his passing, making Love In Vein has taken on an even deeper meaning for me. I want to honor his voice and the rawness of the book without softening its edges,” said De Los Santos. For Hanley, the production marks a return to working with the Downey family. Hanley previously produced Two Girls and a Guy , starring Robert Downey Jr.

“I’m thrilled to be making another film with a Downey. I produced Two Girls and a Guy with Robert many years ago, and now getting to work with Indio on Love In Vein feels like a wonderful full-circle moment. Indio brings exactly the vulnerability and authenticity this role needs,” said Hanley.

Musician Indio, 33, is the eldest of Robert Downey Jr’s three children. He previously had fleeting parts in a handful of movies, including Kiss Kiss Bang Bang , starring his father. In an echo of the themes central to Love In Vein , Downey Jr. famously experienced his own addiction issues in the ’90s, which he overcame on his way to becoming one of the world’s highest-paid and most in-demand actors.

article_text:
大河ドラマ「豊臣兄弟！」で注目を集めている豊臣秀吉。主人公・豊臣秀長の兄として、ストーリーに大きく関わる人物です。そんな秀吉を茶道史の側面から紹介した矢部良明さんの本『茶人 豊臣秀吉』がＫＡＤＯＫＡＷＡから刊行されています。

茶道界では、千利休を切腹させたダークなイメージのある秀吉ですが、本書では「桃山茶の湯のプロモーターだった」と評価。利休のプロモーションを行い、新しい茶の湯トレンドを生み出した“最強プロモーター・秀吉”の正体について、陶磁器・茶道史研究家の矢部さんが、同時代の史料研究をもとに解き明かしています。

破天荒なイベントを次々と企画！

茶が大好きだった秀吉が、はじめて織田信長から茶の湯開催を許されたのは、三木城攻略中だった天正6年（1578）。城近くの本陣で開いた初茶会で、秀吉は堺から大御所茶人の津田宗及を招き、信長から拝領した名物茶道具を並べ、豪華な白鳥汁も用意。初の自主イベントに張り切っていたようです。

信長存命中は、上司に遠慮しながら伝統的な茶道をたしなんでいた秀吉ですが、本能寺の変以降、茶会を自分好みのやり方に変えていきます。

「侘び、寂び」を重んじる利休から茶の湯の美学を学んだ秀吉は、「天下万民、茶のもとですべての人は平等」と考え、誰もが参加できる伝統破りの茶会を企画。さらに、宮中で茶会を開くという前代未聞のイベントも実施し、利休創案の茶の湯を発展させていきます。

茶会の詳細については、ぜひ本書をご覧ください。醍醐の花見をはじめ、大小さまざまな茶会における秀吉の多彩なアイデアが紹介され、読んでいてワクワクします。

茶の湯界のエンターテイナー

また、茶道具についても、秀吉のプロモーターぶりが発揮されています。利休は四民平等の思想のもと、経済力がなく唐物名物を持てない一般茶人を助けるため、創作茶道具を開発。それらを天下人の秀吉が強力にバックアップすることで、利休の茶道具は権威づけされ、世の中に浸透しました。

興味深いのは、「秀吉は建前として利休を支持しただけで、自分の茶会では創作茶道具をほとんど使わず、伝統的な名物を用いた」という事実。その結果、天下人御用達となった唐物は一段と箔づけされ、名物を骨格とした高級武家茶道が確立されました。この点について、著者は「秀吉の隠れた文化面での功績」と讃えています。

名物を好むいっぽうで、秀吉は「黄金の茶席」や「黄金の茶道具」もつくり、派手な装束を身につけ、気ままな茶会も開いています。厳かな茶の湯だけではおもしろくないと考えた秀吉は、茶の湯美学を理解しながらも、時にはあえて作法を無視して、エンターテイナーとして人々を楽しませていました。

茶の湯革命を起こした天下人

利休創作茶の湯を発展させ、武家茶道の原型を定め、さらに楽しい茶会イベントも開いた秀吉。この時代の茶道といえば利休がメインで、天下人は脇役のイメージでしたが、秀吉こそが茶の湯革命を起こした主役だったのです。著者は「今日に至る茶の湯の礎を決定した中心人物は秀吉だった」と結んでいます。

大河ドラマで注目されている今こそ、本書で秀吉の茶人としての功績に触れてみてはいかがでしょうか。

『茶人 豊臣秀吉』は定価1,540円。 KADOKAWAオフィシャルサイト などで購入できます。

著者紹介：矢部良明（やべ・よしあき）さん 1943年、神奈川県生まれ。東北大学文学部美術史科修了。陶磁器・茶道史研究家。東京国立博物館工芸課長、郡山市立美術館館長、薩摩伝承館、人間国宝美術館館長を歴任。著書に、『茶の湯とやきもの』（ＫＡＤＯＫＡＷＡ）、『すぐわかる茶の湯の名品茶碗』（東京美術）、『秀吉 VS. 利休 ― 和合と、破局と ―』（宮帯出版社）など多数。2026年、逝去。

（ライター・田代わこ）

article_text:
Kristina Rozhkova’s photobook blurs the boundaries between bodies, species, powers

A man holds a goose: one hand grips its neck; the other pins back its wings. In another image, another pair of hands pulls back a dog’s lips to expose its sharp, white teeth. Elsewhere, live rats are stuffed into a glass jar; the organs of gutted fish spill across a table; a thick metal chain is tightened around a man’s neck and humans suck the toes of other humans. In Kristina Rozhkova’s photobook, images of human and nonhuman bodies rub up against one another – feeding, breeding, hurting, restraining.

As you flip through the pages of this compact publication, the boundary between species blur; however civilised we might imagine ourselves to be, animal instincts remain part of human life. Many of the mixture of black-and-white and colour shots included here are stark and gory scenes of control and vulnerability in their own right. Through their sequencing, however, they acquire a sinister charge. A child’s gappy mouth, new teeth pushing through gleaming pink gums, sits opposite white rodents in a pink metal cage; images of breastfeeding appear alongside calves at udders and industrial milking equipment.

Cages, ropes, traps and harnesses appear throughout, but their meanings keep shifting: a body might be held against its will or it might be engaged in consensual BDSM play. In a short text at the back of the book, Rozhkova recalls growing up around dogs bred by her mother: ‘I loved sitting in a dog crate, feeling it was my own little house.’ A cage can signify shelter as readily as confinement. That distinction became more fraught, we learn, when, in 2024, the photographer was detained following a semi-nude photoshoot at a St Petersburg cemetery, and charged with desecrating burial sites. She spent two months in detention before being transferred to house arrest. Gut Feeling is strongest, though, when the images leave us to negotiate the difference between restraint, comfort, submission and coercion. Violence and control, the photos suggest, is not always legible from a gesture itself; its meaning depends on context, control and choice.

Gut Feeling by Kristina Rozhkova. Void , €50 (hardcover)
